_why_two_claims: AGREEMENT asks whether the engines compute the same thing; RECOVERY asks whether they compute the right thing. Agreement alone passes identical mistakes. Recovery alone passes a default mismatch smaller than sampling error.
_why_not_self_generated: Expected values are not recorded from running this code. The fixture draws the outcome from a LOGIT-link model, so the conditional log odds ratio the generator uses is exactly the parameter logistic regression estimates, and the truth is a property of the data rather than of any implementation.

agreement.claim: every executed engine reproduces the same coefficients, the same model-based standard error, and the same PROFILE-LIKELIHOOD and WALD interval bounds
agreement._note: 1e-4, the library default, and MEASURED against this entry rather than inherited. Observed spread across R 4.6.1 and Python 3.9 on identical rows: 0.0 on both coefficients, 1.4e-7 on the standard error, and at worst 5.9e-7 on a profile bound -- so the tolerance sits about 170x above the noise floor. The interval bounds are the point of this entry and needed the measurement: R's confint.glm interpolates the profile crossing with a spline while the Python file solves for the root with brentq, and it was not obvious in advance that two different procedures would land within 6e-7 of each other.
agreement._what_this_catches: Substituting a WALD bound where a PROFILE one is claimed moves profile_lo by 2.3e-4, which is 2.3x this tolerance and is therefore caught. That margin is thinner than the 40x the modified-Poisson entry has against an HC0/HC3 swap, and the reason is worth stating rather than hiding: at n=4000 with 946 events the two intervals genuinely have almost converged. They separate when events are few -- which is exactly the situation in which the choice between them matters most, and exactly where this entry's fixture is least able to demonstrate it.

recovery.claim: the estimates are close to the conditional log odds ratio and covariate coefficient the fixture used
recovery._note: MEASURED, three observed standard errors for each key rather than one number serving both. The exposure SE is 0.0817 (3 SE = 0.245, so 0.25) and the covariate SE is 0.0427 (3 SE = 0.128, so 0.13). A single 0.25 applied to the covariate would be nearly six of ITS standard errors. That is not a hypothetical: the probit negative control below misses the covariate by 0.200, which 0.13 catches and a shared 0.25 would have passed in silence. Observed misses on the real files: 0.0664 on the exposure log odds ratio (0.81 SE) and 0.0154 on the covariate (0.36 SE).
recovery._why_not_tighter: The recovery claim is deliberately loose because an estimate carries sampling error. It exists to catch an implementation that agrees with another implementation on the same wrong model -- a probit fit, an inverted response level, or an unadjusted fit standing in for an adjusted one. RUN, not argued. Three negative controls were fitted against the real R output and each fails: an unadjusted fit (crude log odds ratio 0.9579, missing truth by 0.2648, over the 0.25 limit), a probit link (misses by 0.3275 on the exposure and 0.2001 on the covariate), and a Wald bound substituted for a profile one (agreement spread 2.3e-4 on profile_lo and 3.1e-4 on profile_hi, over the 1e-4 limit). The Wald substitution is caught by AGREEMENT alone and by neither recovery check, which is the division of labour the two claims exist for.

stata.reason: no Stata licence; and Stata reports Wald limits with no built-in profile-likelihood interval, so its bounds would not be comparable with the executed engines' profile bounds even if it ran

derived_truth.note: Interpretation only; recovery is checked on the log scale in truth. The three odds ratios are three different numbers from one dataset and none is an error. 2.0000 is the CONDITIONAL odds ratio, which is what logistic regression estimates and what truth states. 2.6062 is the crude odds ratio, and its distance from 2.0 is confounding, since exposure depends on the covariate. 1.9403 is the marginal odds ratio obtained by standardising the TRUE model over the observed covariate distribution: no confounding remains in that comparison and it is still not 2.0, which is what NON-COLLAPSIBILITY means. 1.6602 is the standardised risk ratio, a different estimand again -- an odds ratio is not a risk ratio, and with a 23.6% event rate it overstates one.
